query: The Argument in the Margins {Your second-hand textbook came with an argument in the margins. Two former owners, decades apart, have been disagreeing about chapter four in ink.|You've reached chapter six, and the margin argument has followed. A third hand has joined in, in green, mostly to tell them both to calm down.|The margins again. You know the three hands now: the furious one, the patient one, the green one who draws small owls.} {Today it's about whether a spell can be "polite".|Today one of them has written "SEE ME AFTER" to the other, forty years late.|{final_year: You wonder who'll own this book after you.|Someone has pressed a flower at the page where they finally agree.}} Add your own note to the argument {You write a careful note siding with the patient one and citing the page. It feels like joining a very old, very slow conversation.|You add a fourth hand, in pencil, and settle the question of polite spells for good. You're sure someone will disagree in thirty years.|You write a small note to the green one, thanking them for the owls. The book feels more yours for it.} Ignore them and read the text {You cover the margins with your hand and read the actual chapter. It's duller than the argument, and you remember more of it.|You read the printed text and resolutely ignore three people shouting in ink. You lose the thread twice anyway.|You read straight through without once looking at the margins, which takes willpower. The chapter goes in; the fun stays out.}
